_comment: Transcriptions of sign photographs, for markers whose text the state never published as data. Each entry records the exact photograph it was read from, so any reader can check it. These are marked text_status='transcribed' in the dataset -- never 'official'. Transcribe verbatim: keep the sign's own wording, spelling, casing and block order, and mark separate panels with a blank line. Do not tidy, summarise or modernise. If a word is genuinely unreadable use [illegible]. Corrections are welcome through the 'Fix a marker entry' issue form.

MT-1.text:
MARYSVILLE MONTANA

IN 1870 THE MINING TOWN OF MARYSVILLE WAS ESTABLISHED AND NAMED FOR THE FIRST PIONEER WOMAN HERE MARY RALSTON BY THOMAS CRUSE OWNER OF THE FAMOUS DRUM LUMMON MINE

BY 1900 THE MARYSVILLE MINING DISTRICT WAS REPORTED TO BE THE RICHEST GOLD MINING AREA IN THE WORLD WITH A PRODUCTION OF $60,000,000 ONE-HALF OF WHICH WAS TAKEN FROM THE DRUM LUMMON MINE

OTHER LOCAL RICH GOLD MINES ALSO PRODUCING AT THAT TIME WERE THE BALD MOUNTAIN BALD BUTTE EMPIRE BELMONT PENOBSCOT GLOSTER AND SHANNON

THE TOWNS POPULATION AT ITS PEAK WAS ESTIMATED TO BE 4000 RESIDENTS THEY HAD THE SERVICE OF TWO RAILROADS AND 60 BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS INCLUDING 2 NEWSPAPERS

ERECTED BY THE MARYSVILLE PIONEERS ASSOCIATION-1970

MT-3.text:
Garnets, Vigilantes and Gold Dredges

The Ruby River was called the Passamari by the Shoshoni Indians and the Stinking Water by the miners in the early 1860's. Later, it was mistakenly renamed the Ruby, although the gems found along its length were actually garnets.

The road through the valley that connected Virginia City and Bannack was the haunt of prospectors, road agents and vigilantes after gold was discovered in Alder Gulch in 1863. The road eventually became known as the Vigilante Trail. During the 1920's, distinctive signs with the dreaded vigilante numbers 3-7-77 on a blue, white and red background marked the trail.

The large gravel piles to the west are the tailings of gold dredging operations that occurred here over a twenty-year period beginning in 1899. The Conrey Placer Mining Company operated monster dredge boats that literally churned the gulch inside-out, creating huge piles of gravel where only a tangle of scrub brush and stunted trees could grow. It was the final chapter in the history of placer mining in Alder Gulch. The gold mined by the dredges financed Harvard University in the early 20th century.

MT-340.text:
The Little Belt Mountains

The three major rock types (igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic) can be seen along a 20-mile stretch of U.S. Highway 89 south of here. They range from very old to relatively young by geologic standards. Cliffs of gray Madison Group limestone, up to 1500 feet thick, are prominent along U.S. 89 where it descends into Monarch from the north. From Monarch to Neihart the sedimentary rocks exposed are progressively older, from 300 million-year-old Madison Group to the 500 million-year-old Flathead Formation. Quartzite from the Flathead Formation was quarried in this area for use as a decorative stone. In the Neihart area, much older (1.8 billion years old) metamorphic rocks were intruded by magma that cooled to produce the Pinto Diorite that is only slightly younger than the surrounding metamorphic rocks. The Pinto Diorite can be recognized by prominent blocky feldspar crystals in a greenish gray groundmass. The Neihart Quartzite, slightly younger than the other metamorphic rocks, but older than the Flathead Formation is exposed at Memorial Falls. This scenic park is about 0.4 miles from the highway a little over 2 miles southeast of Neihart. The youngest rock seen from the highway is a syenite, a close geologic relative of granite. Only about 50 million years old, the syenite forms craggy exposures along the east side of the highway a little more than eight miles north of Neihart.

The Y-G Be Line

Montana’s highways once had names instead of numbers. The Yellowstone-Glacier Bee Line Highway Association formed in 1915 to develop and promote an automobile route between Gardiner at the north entrance to Yellowstone National Park and Browning near Glacier National Park. Today, U.S. 89 follows the route of the old Y-G Bee Line Highway. The highway was one of thirteen named highways that crisscrossed Montana in the 1910s and 1920s. Formed primarily to promote tourist travel between the national parks, the named highways also advertised businesses along their routes in promotional brochures. The road had colorful names like Yellowstone Trail, Roosevelt Highway, Vigilante Trail, and Custer Battlefield Highway. Each blazed their routes with distinctive symbols, so that motorists could follow them to their destination. The Y-G Bee Line Highway’s symbol consisted of a rectangle divided in half by the color yellow at the top and black at the bottom. The Y-G Bee Line Highway Association remained active promoting good roads in Montana long after the route was designated U.S. 89.

Intrusive igneous rock – Tertiary age

Neihart Quartzite – Precambrian age

Pinto Diorite – Precambrian age

Gneiss – Precambrian age

Volcanic rock – Tertiary age

Jefferson Formation – limestone and dolomite – Devonian age

Geo-facts: • The communities of Monarch and Neihart originated as mining camps in 1882. Prospectors discovered silver and lead in the surrounding mountains in 1881. Gold and zinc was also mined in the area. • Some magma forced its way between layers of sedimentary rock to create blisters or pockets of molten rock called laccoliths. The conduits that fed the magma into the laccoliths radiate out from them like spokes on a wheel and are called dikes. The laccoliths look like flat topped buttes and the dikes are the giant rock walls that lead to them.

Geo-activity:

Neihart in the Fall of 1892.

• As you travel along the highway between Monarch and Neihart, imagine what this area was like more than a 100 years ago when the mines were active. What kinds of minerals do you think they dug from the mines?
